posts.text: Since Claude Code is nearly useless to me until these new draconian rate limits go away (note: I'm not talking about usage limits; these are limits on the number of requests per minute, basically penalizing the use of concurrent agents), I thought I'd list the 3 biggest features from Claude Code that I miss in Codex. Hopefully @thsottiaux and crew can close these gaps soon, since I've had to move almost all of my work over to Codex instead of half of it like I normally do: 1) Ctrl-R to search across all your previously entered messages in that project... 2) No built-in looping/cron functionality. This is just incredibly useful for having CC manage a swarm of agents for me using my ntm (named_tmux_manager) tool. With CC, I can give it the high-level goal and tell it to check in with the swarm every 3 minutes and give instructions to any agents that are idle or need to be restarted. Then I can come back 5 hours later, and a massive amount of useful work has been done. Codex requires babysitting or just queuing up messages, which is much worse. 3) Hooks. I know there's finally some motion on this now, but what I specifically miss are the pre-tool use hooks so I can get my dcg (destructive_command_guard) tool working in Codex finally. I really like both models and harnesses and hope desperately that Anthropic can get its affairs in order and fix this show-stopping issue for me and others who use swarms in our workflows. Right now, it's basically not usable.
posts.notes: HIGHEST SIGNAL. Rate-limit critique thread — CC per-minute request limits penalize concurrent agent workflows, forced migration to Codex. Names 3 killer CC features missing in Codex: Ctrl-R session-message search, looping/cron for autonomous swarm management, pre-tool hooks for dcg. Key operational insight: ntm + CC loop = 5-hour unattended swarm runs; Codex requires babysitting. Directly relevant to orchestrator rate-limit considerations. 49K views, 185 bookmarks, 60 replies. Viral critique.

posts.text: Here you can see what this is starting to look like. Instead of just having a big grid of tmux panes, ntm now lets you press F12 to bring up the ntm HUD, which lets you monitor what's happening... As I keep saying, removing yourself as the bottleneck from the process is the only way to scale up to 100+ agents. And that's sort of the new 'agent-level bitter lesson': the more agents you can usefully harness, the more compute and tokens you're commanding, the more you can do productively.

posts.text: I wanted to give a quick, self-contained example of how rapidly I can now develop useful, polished, well-documented software to solve a problem. In this case, about an hour or so... The problem: my friend @exhaze has been working on some cool formal verification stuff and had some issues he wanted to flag to me about asupersync... I start informally by asking ChatGPT the following: 'Suppose someone wants to post github issues for my project publicly but with encrypted messages... What's the best, easiest to use, off-the-shelf open source way to do this using ECC?' This quickly yielded a good answer, so I then fired up Claude Code and pasted in the output from ChatGPT and asked it to actually build the thing... what I think is interesting is how much further I pushed everything, resulting in a highly polished and well-documented script, and article explaining how to use it, and a skill for agents to help them use it... I used a slick feature in my cass (coding_agent_session_search) tool that lets you export agent sessions as nicely formatted, self-contained, static html files which are easy to serve via GitHub Pages... And THAT is the difference between what anyone might whip up and what I can extract from Claude Code with a bit more time and effort and work on my part. Notice in the session log the sheer number of times and different ways I asked it to review its code and the writeup, and how many times that caused it to find new and different bugs and problems and edge cases and fix them. I see people complain about how Opus sucks at coding, but I am positive that they aren't doing this sort of thing... Also notice how much time I spent making sure that everything was highly optimized for consumption by coding agents... If you aren't extremely focused on this aspect of things in all your tooling, you're making a big mistake, since these tools are increasingly going to be used ONLY by agents, and their opinion matters!
posts.notes: HIGHEST-SIGNAL THREAD. Live case study: 1-hour build of encrypted GitHub issues system via ChatGPT planning → Claude Code execution → ridiculous review loops → fresh-VM end-to-end test. Key methodology insights: (1) iterative review loops catch edge cases, (2) no substitute for real-world deployment testing (even 100 static reviews miss installer bugs), (3) optimize tool docs/UX FOR AGENTS, not humans. 'These tools are increasingly going to be used ONLY by agents, and their opinion matters!' Includes public static HTML session log via cass export. 263 bookmarks, highest in month. Strong ingest candidate for methodology catalogue.
